title: Rapid and scalable synthesis of bismuth dendrites on copper mesh as a high-performance cathode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate
abstract: Bi-based electrode is believed to be one of the promising cathodes for the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. However, it suffers from energyand/or time-consuming preparation process and mass transfer limitation of the reactants. Here, we fabricated a novel networked Bi-based electrode by formed in situ from Bi dendrites integrated into a Cu mesh substrate via a facile replacement reaction with energy and time savings. The asprepared electrode was directly used as a cathode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate without further treatment. It exhibits a formate Faraday efficiency of ≈ 100 %. Additionally, partial current density for formate is as high as 68.51 ± 4.04mA cm. This performance outperforms other results obtained on Bi-based electrodes—even most gas-diffusion electrodes under similar conditions. The excellent performance seen here is most likely attributed to its large surface area and fast transport of the reactants. This originates from the Bi dendrites catalysts and the unique network structure of the Cu mesh substrate. This work offers a facile route to obtain an efficient and robust electrode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate, which makes it easy to scale up in industrial applications.

Rapid and scalable synthesis of bismuth dendrites on copper mesh as a highperformance cathode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate

A B S T R A C T
Bi-based electrode is believed to be one of the promising cathodes for the electroreduction of CO2 to formate. However, it suffers from energy- and/or time-consuming preparation process and mass transfer limitation of the reactants. Here, we fabricated a novel networked Bi-based electrode by formed in situ from Bi dendrites integrated into a Cu mesh substrate via a facile replacement reaction with energy and time savings. The asprepared electrode was directly used as a cathode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate without further treatment. It exhibits a formate Faraday efficiency of ≈ 100 %. Additionally, partial current density for formate is as high as 68.51 ± 4.04mA cm-2. This performance outperforms other results obtained on Bi-based electrodes—even most gas-diffusion electrodes under similar conditions. The excellent performance seen here is most likely attributed to its large surface area and fast transport of the reactants. This originates from the Bi dendrites catalysts and the unique network structure of the Cu mesh substrate. This work offers a facile route to obtain an efficient and robust electrode for electroreduction of CO2 to formate, which makes it easy to scale up in industrial applications.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The electroreduction of CO2 in aqueous solutions has received great attention because it can reduce atmospheric CO2 concentrations [1–3]. It can also produce useful carbon-based fuels under mild conditions (e.g., moderate temperature and atmospheric pressure) [2–4]. Formic acid/formate (depending on pH, “formate” is used hereafter to represent both forms) is a common electroreduction of CO2 product [3]. Compared to gaseous products such as hydrocarbons and CO, formate can be easily stored and transported. Furthermore, formate is a highvalue chemical intermediate and hydrogen storage material [5,6]. The electroreduction of CO2 to formate (ERCF) is appealing industrially [7–10]. However, there are still some challenges in large-scale ERCF [11–13]. One of the key challenges is the development of high-performance electrode materials [11–15].
Various metal-based electrodes (such as Pd, Pb, Hg, Cd, In, Tl and Sn) have been extensively investigated for ERCF [11,14–21]. Unfortunately, these electrodes usually suffer from one or more of the following problems: toxicity, environmental pollution, poor product selectivity, low catalytic activity, low availability, and high cost [11,22]. More recently, bismuth (Bi)-based electrodes have received
great attention for ERCF because Bi is a non-toxic and low-cost material. It also exhibits high selectivity toward ERCF [23–25]. Several Bibased catalysts such as Bi nanosheets [23], Bi nanospheres [25], and nanowires [25] have been developed for ERCF. In order to fabricate Bibased electrodes, the as-prepared Bi-based catalysts are usually coated onto a conductive substrate (e.g., carbon paper) with insulating binder (e.g., Nafion) [23–25]. This electrode preparation procedure is complicated. Moreover, the insulating binder will lower the electrical conductivity of the electrode leading to deterioration in electrode performance [26–28]. In addition, the synthesis of Bi-based catalysts is generally highly energy- and time-consuming. It either requires stateof-the-art synthesis methods and/or large amounts of energy (e.g., thermal energy) [25,26]. These problems limit large-scale applications of Bi-based electrodes.
There are several Bi-based electrodes that are fabricated via directly electrodeposition of Bi-based catalysts (e.g., Bi nanoflakes, Bi dendrites) on a flat conductive substrate (e.g., copper foil) [29–33]. This electrode preparation method avoids the employment of a binder and simplify the electrode synthetic procedure. Nevertheless, it also requires electrical energy.

processes, current Bi-based electrodes often suffer from mass transfer limitation of the reactants, especially at regions of high current density [28,34]. This reduces the advantages of Bi-based electrodes. As a result, the enhancement of mass transport appears to be an important factor for improving ERCF performance. Unfortunately, few efforts have focused on this issue [10,28–34]. It has demonstrated that gas-diffusion electrode has the potential to enhance mass transfer [28,35]. However, it requires complex fabricating technique to assemble different porous layers for optimal electrode performance [35]. Consequently, a rapid, scalable and cost-effective synthesis of high-performance Bi-based electrodes with enhanced mass transfer is still an urgent need and important for large-scale production in ERCF.
Herein, we report a novel networked Bi-based electrode (N-Bi) for ERCF. The N-Bi was prepared by in situ synthesis of Bi dendrites on a Cu mesh substrate via a facile replacement reaction. This process requires no additional energy supply. Moreover, it occurs simply by immersing a substrate in the solution that contains the ionic precursors of metal to be deposited [36]. Thus, this fabrication procedure is energy and time savings vs. the traditional preparation method for Bi-based electrode. The electrode structure of this type will facilitate electron transfer because it avoids the use of a Nafion binder [12]. The Cu mesh was selected as the conductive substrate based on the following considerations: 1) it is a highly conductive and low-cost substrate; 2) the unique open area of the Cu mesh benefits the flow of electrolyte and provides an extra lateral surface vs. the traditional flat conductive substrate of Cu foil [37]. The N-Bi was characterized and its performance for ERCF was studied. Moreover, the performance stability of the N-Bi for ERCF was monitored. Bi-based catalysts were loaded on the Cu foil (T-Bi) via the same procedure as the N-Bi. The performance of the T-Bi for ERCF was also studied as a control.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and chemicals
sections.text: Cu mesh (60 mesh) was obtained from Shanghai Hengxin Co. Ltd. The Cu foil was obtained from Jiangsu Taike Co. Ltd. The Bi(NO3)3, SnCl2 2H2O, KHCO3, and other chemicals were of analytical reagent grade and were obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd. All chemicals were used as purchased without further treatment.

sections.heading: 2.2. Fabrication procedure of the N-Bi
sections.text:
Cu mesh and Cu foil were first immersed in dilute hydrochloric acid (10 wt%) for 10min and subsequently washed with deionized water several times to remove surface impurities before use.
The N-Bi was fabricated as follows. First, the pretreated Cu mesh was immersed into a solution containing 0.25M sulfuric acid, 0.03M stannous sulfate, and 0.6 M thiourea for 10min at room temperature. The as-obtained material was then plunged into 0.05M Bi(NO3)3 for 8min at room temperature. After washing with deionized water several times, the final material was dried at 333 K for 24 h under vacuum. The T-Bi was fabricated via the same procedure as the N-Bi. Specifically, the pretreated Cu foil was first immersed in 0.25M sulfuric acid solution containing 0.6M thiourea and 0.03M stannous sulfate for 10min at room temperature. The as-obtained material was then plunged into 0.05M Bi(NO3)3 for 8min at room temperature. Finally, the as-fabricated material was dried at 333 K for 24 h under vacuum. The catalyst loading amount of the N-Bi and T-Bi were determined through weight difference between initial and final weight [38].

sections.heading: 2.3. Physical characterization
sections.text:
A scanning electron microscope (SEM, S-4800) was used to observe the morphology of the samples. The resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of the samples were performed with a JEOL-
2100 TEM. The crystal structure of the samples was studied with X-ray diffraction (XRD, Smart Lab 9 KW) with Cu Kα radiation. The chemical composition and the valence states of the samples were evaluated with X-ray photoelectron spectra (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi) with Al Kα radiation (1486.6 eV) as the excitation source. All binding energies were referenced to C 1s (284.5 eV).

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical tests procedures and calculations
sections.text:
The electrochemical tests were performed with a CHI600E electrochemical workstation (Shanghai Chenhua, China) in an undivided three-electrode glass cell (Fig. S1). The as-fabricated N-Bi (1 cm2) was the working electrode. A platinum wire was the counter electrode. An Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode was the reference electrode. The measured potential was converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale using the Nernst equation: E(vs. RHE) = E(vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197+0.059 × pH [27]. All of the potential values were in reference to RHE unless otherwise noted.
Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) measurements were done in N2and CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 solution from −0.2 to −1.2 V at a scan rate of 5mV s-1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were performed in CO2-saturated electrolyte from 100 kHz to 0.1 Hz. The Nyquist plots were analyzed by Zsimpwin software (ver. 3.10). The electroactive surface area (EASA) of the astested electrodes were estimated by measuring the double layer capacitance [39]. Cyclic voltammetry was recorded for the working electrode from 0.74 to 0.54 V at different scan rates in N2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 solution. The capacitance (C) was calculated according to the equation: C = current density/scan rate. EASA was calculated by EASA = C × GSA/C0, where C0 is the specific capacitance of a flat standard electrode with 1 cm2 of real surface area (C0= 40 μF cm-2 [39]); GSA is the geometrical area (GSA=1 cm2).
The mass transfer coefficient (Kd) was obtained using ferro/ferricyanide redox couple (5 mM K4[Fe3(CN)6] and 5mM K3[Fe3(CN)6]) in 0.5 M NaOH solution [37,40,41]. When the potential of the as-tested electrode was controlled in the plateau zone of the ferricyanide reduction, the obtained reduction current was diffusion controlled and related to: iL = n × F × S × DOX × COX, S/δ, where iL is the diffusion current (in A), n is the exchanged electrons per anion number (n =1), F is the Faraday constant (96,485 C mol-1), S is the geometric surface area (1×10-4 m2), DOX is the ferricyanide’ diffusion coefficient (0.9× 10- 9 m2 s-1), COX, S is the ferricyanide’ bulk solution concentration (5mM), and δ is the diffusion layer thickness (in m). Then, Kd was calculated by Kd = iL/(n × F × S ×COX, S).
The ERCF tests were carried out in CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 solution. The time of each electrolysis test was 30min. During each test, CO2 was purged into the electrolyte at a flow rate of 20mL min-1. After each test, liquid products were analyzed via an ICS-1500 ion chromatograph (Dionex, USA) using an AS14 (4mm×250mm) separation column. The mobile phase was a mixed aqueous solution of NaHCO3 (0.8 mM) and Na2CO3 (4.5 mM). Figures of merit including Faraday efficiency (FEformate) and partial current density for formate (Jformate) were used to assess ERCF performance. FEformate was defined as the percentage of the total charge supplied to produce formate [27]. Jformate was defined as the current supplied to produce formate divided by the geometric area of the as-tested electrode [9,10,23,26,29].

sections.heading: 3.1. Fabrication and characterization of the N-Bi
sections.text:
In principle, a reactant with a lower redox potential can replace another reactant with higher redox potential in solutions. However, the redox potential of either Cu+/Cu (0.521 V vs. normal hydrogen electrode, NHE) or Cu2+/Cu (0.342 V vs. NHE) is higher than that of Bi3+/ Bi (0.308 V vs. NHE) [42,43]. Therefore, the direct replacement of Bi3+
by Cu is thermodynamically unfavorable. Previous studies have shown that Cu can replace Sn2+ with a thiourea ligand [9]. Meanwhile, the replacement of Bi3+ by Sn is warranted because of the lower redox potential of Sn2+/Sn (−0.137 V vs. NHE) vs. Bi3+/Bi (0.308 V vs. NHE). Here, we used a two-step replacement reaction to fabricate the N-Bi (Fig. 1). Briefly, Sn was first loaded onto the Cu mesh (Sn/Cu mesh) via a replacement reaction between Cu and Sn2+ with a thiourea ligand (replacement reaction 1: Sn2+ + 2Cu + 8[SC(NH2)2] → Sn +2{Cu[SC(NH2)2]4}+). Subsequently, the Bi3+ was replaced by Sn (replacement reaction 2: 2Bi3+ + 3Sn → 2Bi + 3Sn2+) to produce the N-Bi. More details related to the fabrication process of the N-Bi were described in the Supporting information (Fig. S2-S3).
The as-fabricated samples were preliminarily characterized by XRD (Fig. 2a). For the Cu mesh, the diffraction peaks at 43.3°, 50.4°, and 74.1° can be indexed to the (111), (200), and (220) planes of Cu [JCPDS# 65–9026]. For the Sn/Cu mesh, the diffraction peaks at 30.6°, 32.0°, 43.9°, and 44.9° can be indexed to the (200), (101), (220), and (211) planes of Sn [JCPDS# 65–2631]. Moreover, the SnO2 (111) peak is observed at 29.9° [JCPDS# 29–1484]. This indicates that Sn has been successfully deposited on a Cu mesh substrate; some deposited Sn particles are oxidized during the preparation process. For the N-Bi, the diffraction peaks of Sn and SnO2 on the Sn/Cu mesh disappear, while the diffraction peaks of Bi appear. The diffraction peaks of Bi at 27.2°, 37.9°, and 39.6° can be indexed to the (012), (104), and (110) planes of Bi [JCPDS# 44–1246]. This verifies the successful synthesis of Bi
particles via the replacement reaction between Sn and Bi3+; the Cu substrate is not completely coated by Bi particles.
To probe the elemental composition and chemical states of Bi particles for the N-Bi, XPS tests were used. The peaks at binding energies of 159.0 and 164.4 eV in Bi 4f XPS spectrum can be assigned to Bi3+ [31] (Fig. 2b). This means that the surface of Bi particles are oxidized. The O 1s peak was deconvolute to clarify the oxidation states of Bi components. The binding energy at 530.9 eV is associated with O-Bi3+ [29]. Thus, the XPS characterization data suggest that Bi particles in the N-Bi exists as Bi2O3. This is different from the XRD results. It is probably because XPS can only parse the valence states of particles in the outer layer of ca. 10 nm of the samples [27].
The as-obtained samples were further characterized by SEM and TEM. Fig. 3a shows that the Cu mesh has a smooth surface. After displacement of Sn for 10min, the sample displays nodular morphology (Fig. 3b). The Sn film thickness is about 2-3 μm (Fig. S4). After displacement of Bi for 8min, the sample presents dendrites structure in which smaller branches grow on bigger branches (Fig. 3c). The corresponding elemental mappings show Bi and Cu elements (Fig. 3d), which is consistent with the XRD results. This implies that the Cu substrate is not completely coated by Bi dendrites. The thickness of Bi dendrites is about 10−15 μm (Fig. 3e–f). The TEM image shows that the Bi catalyst has dendrites structure (Fig. 3g). The lattice fringe spacing is estimated to be 0.228 nm in high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 3h). This matches with (110) plane of Bi indicating the formation of Bi phase, which is
consistent with the XRD patterns in Fig. 2a. The physical characterization results imply that Bi dendrites are in situ produced on the Cu mesh substrate via a two-step reaction. The Bi dendrites exist as Bi and Bi2O3—the former is inside the Bi dendrites and the latter is on the exterior. The oxide layer on the surface of the Bi dendrites catalysts can inhibit the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and thus be beneficial to ERCF [30]. The Bi dendrites catalyst is
promising for ERCF due to its large surface area and high degree of connectivity accompanied by a large amount of active sites [33]. Its advantages have been demonstrated in previous works [31–33]. Nevertheless, the as-fabricated Bi dendrites catalysts in previous works are synthesized via an electrodeposition method that requires electrical energy supply. This is different from our work.
With aim to understand Bi dendrites growth process on Cu mesh, we
investigated surface morphologies of the as-obtained samples with different reaction times. For Sn loading process, some Sn nanoparticles appear when the replacement time is 1min (Fig. S5a). The size of Sn nanoparticles increases as the replacement time increases from 1min to 2min (Fig. S5b). When the replacement time increases further to 6min, the sample displays nodular morphology (Fig. S5c), which is the same as that of 10min (Fig. 3b). For Bi dendrites growth process, it can be seen that when the replacement time is 2min, scattered Bi nanoparticles appear (Fig. S6a). As prolong the reaction time to 5min, some Bi nanoparticles grow into randomly arranged dendrites (Fig. S6b). When the reaction time reaches 8min, the Bi dendrites grow longer and denser and the substrate is coated by Bi dendrites (Fig. 3c). Therefore, a possible growth process of Bi dendrites for the N-Bi is proposed in Fig. S7. When Cu mesh is immersed in SnSO4 solution, the replacement reaction between Cu and Sn2+ occurs with the aid of thiourea (Sn2+ + 2Cu + 8[SC(NH2)2] → Sn +2{Cu[SC(NH2)2]4}+). This process produces Sn/Cu mesh. When the Sn/Cu mesh is immersed in Bi(NO3)3 solution, replacement reaction 2 (2Bi3+ + 3Sn → 2Bi + 3Sn2+) takes place, resulting in the formation of Bi crystals as nuclei. And then, innumerable primary cells are formed spontanously. The primary cells consist of Sn anode, Bi cathode, and NO3- solution as electrolyte. The half-cell reaction is as follows: 1/2Sn － e- → 1/2Sn2+ (anode); 1/ 3Bi3+ + e- → 1/3Bi (cathode). The subsequent growth of Bi crystals will preferentially occur on the preformed Bi nuclei via a primary cell reaction rather than the direct surface replacement reaction. This is possibly due to the relatively high activation energy of the surface reaction vs. primary cell reaction [44]. The continuous cathode reaction leads to form the dendrites structure.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical performance of the N-Bi for ERCF
sections.text:
LSV measurements were conducted initially to explore the electrochemical performance of the N-Bi and T-Bi (Fig. 4a). Generally, only HER occurs in N2-saturated electrolyte, but both HER and ERCF occur in CO2-saturated electrolyte [16,27]. Obviously, the reduction currents obtained in CO2-saturated electrolyte are larger than those in N2-saturated electrolyte over the N-Bi and T-Bi. This indicates that the N-Bi and T-Bi have an obvious catalytic activity for ERCF. In addition, the N-Bi and T-Bi exhibit similar HER currents; the N-Bi exhibits larger current in CO2-saturated electrolyte than the T-Bi. This implies that the N-Bi can enhance the catalytic activity toward reduction reactions mainly acting on ERCF due to the similar HER currents between the N-Bi and TBi.
In order to explore the selectivity of ERCF, the ratio of reduction current in CO2-saturated electrolyte to the reduction current in N2-saturated electrolyte (i.e., IERCF+HER/IHER) was calculated [45]. A value greater than one suggests that the electrode is selective for ERCF [45]. As seen from Fig. S8, the value of IERCF+HER/IHER obtained from the N-
Bi is larger than that of the T-Bi at a potential more negative than ca.−0.5 V. For example, the N-Bi displays a value of 4.12 at −1.2 V, which is 162 % higher than the T-Bi (1.57). This means that the N-Bi can enhance the selectivity of ERCF vs. the T-Bi.
The electrochemical performance of the as-investigated electrodes were further performed via stepped-potential electrolysis at each given potential (Fig. 4b–c). It can be seen that Faraday efficiency for formate (FEformate) obtained from the Cu mesh is very low, indicating the Cu mesh almost has no catalytic activity for ERCF. This is supported by the previous conclusion that Cu possessed high catalytic activity for electroreduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons not formate in aqueous solutions [11]. Thus, for the N-Bi, only the Bi dendrites are active in ERCF.
For the N-Bi, formate is first reproducibly detected at −0.76 V with a FEformate of 1.52 ± 0.02 % (Fig. 4b). It quickly increases to> 80 % at −1.06 V and peaks close to 100 % at −1.26 V. It then starts to slowly decline at more negative potential due to an increase in HER—this competes with ERCF [9]. In contrast, FEformate for the T-Bi takes off at −0.96 V, which is 200mV more negative than that of the N-Bi. This suggests that a higher overpotential is needed for ERCF on the T-Bi than that on the N-Bi. FEformate is highest (69.48 ± 5.22 %) also at −1.26 V, which is 29 % lower than that for the N-Bi.
Other than FEformate, partial current density for formate (Jformate) were calculated and plotted against the applied potential as shown in Fig. 4c. The N-Bi delivers higher Jformate than the T-Bi under each applied potential. For instance, the Jformate for the N-Bi at the applied potential of −1.26 V is 68.51 ± 4.04mA cm-2. In contrast, at that applied potential, the T-Bi shows a Jformate of 25.19 ± 2.22mA cm-2, which is 63 % lower than that of the N-Bi.
The electrochemical tests results presented above suggest a significant improvement in ERCF performance for the N-Bi vs. the T-Bi. A straightforward hypothesis for the enhancement is higher electroactive surface area (EASA) because a larger EASA could afford more catalytically active sites [24,46]. To verify this hypothesis, the EASAs of the as-tested electrodes were estimated via by measuring the double layer capacitance (Fig. 5a-c) [39]. The EASA of the N-Bi is measured to be 35.75 cm2, which is 24 % larger than that of the T-Bi (28.75 cm2). The increase in EASA for the N-Bi is likely due to the Cu mesh substrate, which provides an extra lateral surface area vs. Cu foil for use in the TBi.
However, the normalized partial current density for formate (Jsformate) obtained from the N-Bi is also 30–133% larger than that of the T-Bi (Fig. 5d). Moreover, the difference of Jsformate between the N-Bi and T-Bi increases with the applied potential. Taking into account the structural changes from the T-Bi to N-Bi, the improvement in the Jsformate may be related with an enhanced reactants concentration in the vicinity of the catalytically active sites. This indicates that the mass transport process is enhanced on the N-Bi vs. the T-Bi. To obtain an insight into the enhancement of mass transfer by the N-Bi, the mass
transfer coefficient (Kd) was estimated (Fig. S9). The Kd for the N-Bi is measured to be 6.47× 10-6 m s-1, which is 16 % larger than that for the T-Bi (5.58× 10-6 m s-1). This confirms that the mass transport process is enhanced by the N-Bi. The enhancement of mass transport is likely due to the network structure of the Cu mesh that improves electrolyte diffusion.
To further investigate the origins of the improvement in ERCF performance for the N-Bi, we used EIS measurements with the N-Bi and T-Bi (Fig. 5e). For the T-Bi, the Nyquist plot shows one semicircle and a sloping line. The semicircle in the high frequency region reflects the charge transfer process during electrochemical reactions [39,47]; the sloping line at the low frequency corresponds to the reactants’ diffusion process [48]. The equivalent circuit model i (Fig. 5f) was used to simulate the obtained Nyquist plot. For the N-Bi, the Nyquist plot shows one semicircle and was modeled by equivalent circuit model ii (Fig. 5f). The fitting results are given in Table S1.
It is worth noting that the Warburg impedance (W) only exists on the T-Bi. This confirms that the mass transport process is enhanced by the N-Bi. In addition, the charge transfer resistance (Rct) value obtained from the N-Bi (24.39 Ω) is 13 % lower than that of the T-Bi (28.13 Ω)
indicating a much faster charge transfer process on the N-Bi [46–48]. The decrease in the Rct value may be related to increased reactants concentration near the catalytically active sites [46]. This could also be attributed to the improved mass transfer of the reactants.
Based on the above results and analysis, it is concluded that the enhanced performance of the N-Bi over the T-Bi toward ERCF is likely due to its large EASA and fast mass transport of the reactants. This originates from the network structure of the Cu mesh substrate. This is to say, the use of network electrode can effectively alleviate the mass transfer limitation for ERCF.
To gain an insight into the possible mechanism of ERCF on the N-Bi, Tafel plot of formate for the N-Bi was obtained at regions of low overpotential, where ERCF is dominated by electrokinetics [33] (Fig. S10). The plot is 95mV dec−1, which is close to the slope of 118mV dec−1 [25,26]. This means that an initial one electron transfer step from electrode to CO2 to form surface adsorbed CO2·- intermediate is the rate-determining step of ERCF [25,26]. According to previously reported results [9,26,30,45,49], a possible mechanism of ERCF on the N-Bi is illustrated as follows:
CO2 (solution) → CO2 (ads) (1)
CO2 (ads) + e- → CO2·- (ads) (2)
CO2·- (ads) +HCO3- + e- → HCOO- (ads) + CO32- (3)
HCOO- (ads) → HCOO- (solution) (4)
CO2 + CO32- +H2O → 2HCO3- (5)
It is useful to compare the performance of the N-Bi with recently reported Bi-based ERCF electrodes under similar conditions (Table S2). The performance of the N-Bi is better than other Bi-based ERCF electrodes. This performance is even larger than those of most gas diffusion electrodes reported previously (see Table S3). The origins for the enhanced performance of the N-Bi toward ERCF are speculated as follows: 1) the associated Bi dendrites catalysts provide large surface area (35.75 cm2 here), which afford many catalytically active sites [33]; 2) fast mass transport of the reactants originated from the network structure; 3) fast electron transfer resulting from the electrode structure of binder-free [12]. The combination of large catalytic activity and high
selectivity of formate observed for the N-Bi is quite useful for practical production—especially when considering the rapid, scalable and costeffective electrode preparation method.

sections.heading: 3.3. The stability of the N-Bi for ERCF
sections.text:
From the point of practical production, sustainable stability is important as well as a high performance. To examine the stability of the NBi for ERCF, ERCF test at a potential of −1.26 V for 30min per run and ten electrolysis runs were performed. The stability testing was conducted by applying the amperometric i–t curve mode. Fig. 6a and b show that there are a slight decrease in FEformate and Jformate.
XRD characterization of the N-Bi after the stability testing shows that the crystal structures of the N-Bi do not change significantly after stability testing (Fig. 6c). The Bi4f XPS shows that there is a ca. 0.3 eV binding energy shift to lower energy for the catalyst after the stability testing (Fig. 6d). This indicates that part of Bi catalysts have been slightly reduced, which is in line with previously reported results [32,50]. Moreover, the dendrites structure of the Bi catalysts is slightly
damaged as seen in SEM (Fig. 6f). Therefore, we inferred that the slight decrease in the ERCF performance is probably due to the change in Bi catalyst surface morphology. This is a known feature of Bi-based ERCF electrodes [29,31,32]. Future research is need to clarify the mechanism of morphological change of Bi dendrites and improve the stability of Bibased ERCF electrodes.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
Bi dendrites catalysts were successfully grown on Cu mesh as a networked Bi-based ERCF electrode (N-Bi) via a facile, energy- and time-saving replacement reaction. The Bi dendrites catalysts provide a large number of active sites for ERCF and the mass transfer of the reactants is enhanced due to the network structure of Cu mesh. Based on the enhancement mechanism, it is found that the N-Bi shows a maximum Faraday efficiency of ca. 100 % and a partial current density of 68.51 ± 4.04mA cm-2 for formate production. These values are among the highest known for ERCF with Bi-based electrodes under similar conditions. This work will be helpful for the potential large-scale application of Bi-based electrodes in EFCF.
